描述_ZN: Lake Dongting and Red Cliff, known as one of China's most famous scenic spots since ancient times, are captured in a single view and depicted using the gold-blue-blue-green landscape painting technique. Many buildings, houses, and figures can be seen in this bird's-eye view of the landscape. From the inscription, it is clear that Ike Taiga (1723-76) was 49 years old when he created this representative work of his later years. This work has many titles and inscriptions, indicating that it was popular among the literati at the time of its creation. First, the title inscription was written by Han Tianshou, a well-known calligrapher and seal engraver, and the inscription "Tang-jin no ho" expresses his admiration for the authentic Tang dynasty-style blue-green landscapes. Next, the title "Qiankun niyoru bui" (Du Fu's "Tengyueyang Lou") by the Chinese scholar Miyazaki Gyunpo evokes the magnificent view of Lake Dongting from the Yueyang Lou. In addition, the rovings are by Hosogai Hansai, a Chinese scholar and poet, and Lai Chunsui, a Chinese scholar. From Hansai's afterword, we learn that this work was commissioned by Nishimura Mengqing, a member of the Chaosha, a Chinese poetry society in Osaka and a merchant, and that Taiga referred to Yang Jizeng's "Newly Chiseled Views of the Interior of the Sea" (published in 1609) when creating this work. Taiga's own praise is also taken from the same book. Chunsui's afterword praises the work as a work that allows the viewer to contemplate and play in the painting (lying down and playing) by comparing it to the scenic beauty of various countries he had experienced in the past. On the other hand, "Ejigoto hikigen" by Taiga's friend, Kuwayama Gyokusu, states that the "water pattern on the lake" in this work is excellent and new, and that Taiga's repeated trips to Lake Biwa to observe the shimmering water was used in its expression. The delicate expression of the water, expressed by the very thinly painted shades of deep blue and the fine lines of sumi ink drawn over them, is indeed a major characteristic of this work. Taiga was a keen student of imported Chinese paintings and frequently used them as references in his work, but it is important to note that he also placed great importance on observation of the actual scene, which is a fundamental aspect of his approach to art making. Nishimura Mengqing, who ordered this work, often performed it at poetry gatherings of the Chaosha, and Ge Ziqin left a poem inspired by this work. The existence of successors to this work by Taiga's disciples, such as "Lake Dotai" by Shukuya Aoki (Fukuoka City Museum of Art) and "Dotai Akakabe" by Gogaku Fukuhara (Osaka Museum of History), shows how widely the work was recognized and enjoyed.
